knowledgePoints.name: Start the answer for it
knowledgePoints.teach:
Asking for “JSON only” gets you JSON wrapped in a helpful sentence. Asking more firmly gets you a shorter sentence.

The mechanical fix is to write the beginning of the assistant turn yourself. Claude continues from where you left it, so the preamble never gets a place to exist:

messages = [
    {"role": "user",      "content": "Extract the invoice fields as JSON."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "```json"},        # ← prefill
]

resp = client.messages.create(
    model=M, max_tokens=1024, messages=messages,
    stop_sequences=["```"],                              # ← stop at the fence
)

data = json.loads(resp.content[0].text.strip())

Prefill removes the preamble. The stop sequence removes the trailing commentary.

The same trick constrains code, lists, or CSV — anything whose delimiter is unambiguous.

questions.q: Claude keeps wrapping requested JSON in a sentence of explanation. Which two moves remove it?
options: Lower the temperature and raise max_tokens
Prefill with an opening fence; stop on close
Move the request into the system prompt block
Enable streaming and parse the first delta
questions.explain: Prefill kills the opening preamble; the stop sequence kills the trailing commentary.

questions.q: How does prefilling actually suppress the preamble?
options: It instructs Claude never to write one
It strips the preamble server-side first
It sets stop_reason to stop_sequence at once
Claude continues from the assistant text
questions.explain: It is continuation, not instruction. The turn has already started, and it started with a fence.

reviewQuestions.q: Besides JSON, what else can prefill plus a stop sequence constrain?
options: Nothing — the technique is JSON-specific
Code, lists, or CSV — anything delimited
Only output whose length is known first
Only tool inputs, never the text output
reviewQuestions.explain: The requirement is an unambiguous delimiter to open with and stop on, not a particular format.

reviewQuestions.q: Which stop_reason do you expect on a successful prefill-and-stop extraction?
options: stop_sequence
end_turn
max_tokens
tool_use
reviewQuestions.explain: Generation ended because it hit the string you supplied.

knowledgePoints.name: The tool that is never called
knowledgePoints.teach:
For production extraction there is a sturdier option than hoping prose parses. Define a tool whose input_schema is the output contract, and read the structured input off the tool_use block:

tools = [{
  "name": "record_invoice",
  "description": "Record the fields extracted from an invoice.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "invoice_number": {"type": "string"},
      "total_cents":    {"type": "integer"},
      "due_date":       {"type": "string", "format": "date"}
    },
    "required": ["invoice_number", "total_cents"]
  }
}]

There need not be a real function behind it. The tool exists so the model has a typed shape to fill, and the API validates the shape on the way out.

Prefill hopes for valid JSON. A schema asks the API to enforce it.

Use a generic to_json-style tool for a quick prototype or changing requirements; use a dedicated schema for complex, high-accuracy production work.

questions.q: Why prefer a tool schema over prefill for high-accuracy production extraction?
options: It costs noticeably fewer output tokens
Tool calls are run on a more capable model
The shape is declared and validated, not hoped
Prefill is unavailable once tools are defined
questions.explain: A schema turns 'please return this shape' into a contract the API checks.

questions.q: When is a generic to_json-style tool the better choice over a dedicated schema?
options: For complex, high-accuracy production work
Whenever more than three fields are needed
When the output has to be deeply nested JSON
For prototypes, or requirements still moving
questions.explain: Generic for speed and churn; dedicated for accuracy and stability.

knowledgePoints.name: Shape is not truth
knowledgePoints.teach:
A JSON Schema validates structure. It has nothing to say about whether the values are right.

The schema catchesThe schema misses
total_cents is a string, not an integertotal_cents is 1200 when the invoice says 12000
due_date is missingdue_date is in the past
an unknown field appearedinvoice_number belongs to a different customer

Validate the returned values in application code. A schema validates shape, not business truth.

This is the same boundary as everywhere else in the section: the model's output is input to your system, and input gets checked.

questions.q: Your extraction tool returns a well-formed record with a total that is off by a factor of ten. What failed?
options: Nothing in the schema; correctness is yours
The schema — it should have bounded the range
The tool_choice setting was set wrongly
The model tier was too small for the maths
questions.explain: Shape passed because the shape was fine. Only application-level validation catches a wrong-but-well-typed value.

questions.q: Which check does a JSON Schema perform?
options: That a supplied date is in the future
That an identifier exists in your database
That a field is present and typed right
That a total matches the sum of line items
questions.explain: Presence and type — structure. The other three are business rules.

reviewQuestions.q: What is the relationship between the tool you define for structured output and a real function?
options: There must be a function; the API calls it
The function must return the declared schema
The function is run server-side by Anthropic
There need not be one; it is a typed shape
reviewQuestions.explain: It is a contract, not necessarily an implementation. You read the tool_use input and never dispatch anything.

knowledgePoints.name: Three settings, three guarantees
knowledgePoints.teach:
tool_choiceguaranteeuse when
autoClaude may call a tool, or may answer in proseClaude should judge whether the tool applies
anySome tool will be calleda tool is required, but which one is Claude's call
naming a toolThat tool will be calledstructured output is mandatory

Force the tool when the endpoint must always return a record. Leave it auto when 'no structured answer applies' is a legitimate outcome.

The failure mode of leaving it on auto for a mandatory-extraction endpoint is intermittent and unpleasant: it works on the clear cases and returns prose on exactly the ambiguous inputs where you most needed a record.

questions.q: An endpoint must always return a filled-in record, never prose. Which tool_choice?
options: The specific tool, named outright — forced
auto, so Claude can decline on bad input
any, so Claude picks the closest tool it has
auto, plus an instruction to always use it
questions.explain: Naming the tool is the only setting that guarantees that tool gets called.

options: Every defined tool gets called exactly once
Some tool is called; Claude picks which
One specific named tool is always called
No tool unless the input is unambiguous
questions.explain: any requires a tool call without dictating which one.

reviewQuestions.q: Your extraction endpoint is on tool_choice auto and returns prose on roughly one request in twenty. What is the fix?
options: Lower temperature, for a steadier choice
Improve the tool description, keep auto
Force the tool by name; it is guaranteed
Retry any prose response until it works
reviewQuestions.explain: If a record is mandatory, do not leave it to judgement. Forcing it is a guarantee rather than a nudge.
